analysis.one_liner: Requires a federal license with training and background checks to buy assault weapons.
analysis.headline: The bill drew no cosponsors, never got a committee vote, and died when the 117th Congress ended in January 2023.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have created a federal license to buy semiautomatic assault weapons, which the bill defines broadly to include AR-15 and AK-style rifles, certain pistols, and shotguns. To get a license, a person would need to pass a background check, complete hands-on firearms safety training, submit fingerprints, pay a $130 fee, and renew every five years. The Justice Department could deny or revoke a license for anyone it found posed a significant danger to themselves or others, with court review available. Private sales of these weapons would have to go through a licensed dealer for a background check, and people who already owned covered guns before the law would be exempt.
analysis.who_benefits: People living around would-be shooters who could be flagged by courts, police, or mental-health and domestic-violence records: the bill lets state and local officials submit information showing an applicant is a danger, and requires denial or revocation based on threats of violence, domestic violence orders, stalking, or similar records. Buyers would also get mandatory safety training. Existing owners, hunters, target shooters, and members of the military or law enforcement are explicitly exempt from the license requirement.
analysis.who_benefits_short: People exposed to gun violence risk

how_it_helps.text: Creates a federal license to purchase or receive an assault weapon, requiring a background check, safety training with hands-on firing tests, fingerprints, and a $130 fee, renewable every five years.

Allows state and local officials to submit information that an applicant poses a significant danger of bodily injury, and directs the Attorney General to deny or revoke licenses based on threats, acts of violence, domestic violence or stalking orders, and similar factors, with court review for denials.
Requires private sales of assault weapons to run through a licensed dealer for a background check, closing the unlicensed-sale channel.

Exempts people who lawfully owned the weapon before enactment, plus active-duty military, law enforcement, corrections officers, and supervised temporary transfers for hunting, target shooting, or self-defense.

analysis.who_pays: Buyers of newly covered semiautomatic rifles, pistols, and shotguns pay a $130 fee, take time off for training and fingerprinting, and wait up to 30 days for a license. The firearms industry faces a smaller customer pool for covered new guns, since only licensed buyers can purchase them, while sales of guns already in private hands are grandfathered. Violations carry fines up to $5,000 and a year in jail for a first offense, and up to $15,000 and five years for repeat offenses.

drawbacks.text: The license costs $130 to apply for or renew, requires hands-on training and fingerprinting, and can take up to 30 days to issue, adding time and money for lawful buyers of covered weapons.

The bill does not ban assault weapons; it licenses them, so a person who passes the check and training could still buy one, and the grandfather clause leaves every covered gun already in circulation untouched.

The Attorney General must keep a record of license holders, which gun-rights critics characterize as a firearms registry, and the license-plus-permit structure resembles permitting systems that in some states have been applied unevenly in practice.
The bill would cover a very long list of specific rifles, pistols, and shotguns by name, raising the practical challenge of keeping a by-name list current as new models are introduced.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The design keeps lawful access open while adding a check for danger: training, a background check, and a way for courts and local officials to flag someone violent. The costs are real but modest for most buyers, though the fee and wait time fall on rural and low-income buyers too. The biggest limit is that grandfathering existing weapons and licensing rather than restricting new ones means the effect on available firepower is gradual, not immediate.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in September 2022, sent to the House Judiciary Committee and then its crime subcommittee, and never came up for a vote before the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023, killing the bill.

narrative.text: Rep. Chris Jacobs, a Republican from New York, introduced the Federal Assault Weapons Licensing Act on September 19, 2022.
The bill was referred to the House Committee on the Judiciary, and on November 1, 2022, to its Subcommittee on Crime, Terrorism, and Homeland Security, where action ended.
No member joined as a cosponsor, and the bill received no committee markup, floor vote, or action in the Senate before the Congress expired.

The bill would have required a federal license to buy an assault weapon, with a background check, firearms safety training, fingerprints, a $130 fee, and five-year renewals, and would have routed private sales through licensed dealers for background checks.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: People who oppose any license requirement for buying rifles and pistols, and gun sellers who avoided a narrower buyer pool for covered new firearms; no new restriction took effect.

for.name: Rep. Chris Jacobs
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on September 19, 2022, and it was referred to committee.

against.name: House Judiciary Committee
against.role: Committee of referral; chaired by Rep. Jerry Nadler (D) in the 117th Congress
against.what_they_did: Never took the bill up for a markup or vote; it sat at the subcommittee level until the Congress ended.

against.name: House members generally
against.role: No member of either party cosponsored the bill (0 cosponsors).
against.what_they_did: None of the 435 House members joined the sponsor, including fellow New York Republicans.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had a lone Republican sponsor and zero cosponsors from either party, so no party bloc ever took a recorded position on it.

industries.note: The bill would have narrowed the pool of legal buyers for newly manufactured covered rifles, pistols, and shotguns to licensed individuals, cutting into sales of the industry's most popular semi-auto lines. People who already owned these guns are exempt, so the effect lands on new sales.
The mandatory safety training with hands-on firing tests would have created required work for firearms trainers and for whoever ran the federal licensing offices in urban and rural areas.
